lesson.title: How a Tree Moves Water to the Top of the Canopy Without a Pump
lesson.summary: This section defines cohesion and adhesion as consequences of water's polarity and hydrogen bonding, and shows how the two properties work together to pull water upward through a tree's xylem and to produce surface tension.
lesson.body:
Cohesion and adhesion are two closely related consequences of the hydrogen bonding described in the previous section, and distinguishing between them is mostly a matter of asking what a water molecule is attracted to. Cohesion refers to the attraction between water molecules and other water molecules, the same hydrogen bonding network described earlier, where the partially positive hydrogen atoms of one water molecule are drawn to the partially negative oxygen atoms of neighboring water molecules. Adhesion refers to the attraction between water molecules and a different substance entirely, such as the wall of a narrow glass tube, the cellulose fibers in a plant cell wall, or the surface of a leaf, whenever that substance is also polar or carries charged regions that water's partial charges can be drawn to.

The clearest large scale demonstration of cohesion is surface tension, the tendency of a water surface to behave almost like a thin, stretched film. At the surface of a body of water, molecules have neighboring water molecules to hydrogen bond with on their sides and below, but not above, so the surface molecules end up pulled disproportionately inward and sideways by cohesive forces, creating a taut layer at the interface with air. This is strong enough that some small organisms exploit it directly: water striders, a group of insects, distribute their weight across their long, water repellent legs and walk on top of a pond's surface without breaking through, supported entirely by the cohesive hydrogen bonding network among the water molecules beneath them.

Cohesion and adhesion combine most dramatically inside the water transport system of tall plants and trees, in narrow tubes called xylem vessels that run from the roots up through the trunk and out to the leaves. As water evaporates from tiny pores in the leaves, a process called transpiration, it pulls the adjoining water molecules in the leaf's xylem upward to replace it, and because of cohesion, those molecules are hydrogen bonded to the water molecules below them, which in turn pull on the molecules below them, creating a continuous, unbroken pull that extends all the way down to the roots. This is often called the cohesion tension mechanism, and it is what allows trees over one hundred meters tall, among the tallest living organisms on Earth, to move water from their roots to their highest leaves without any pump, muscular or mechanical, doing the work directly. Adhesion contributes as well, since water molecules are also attracted to the polar cellulose walls lining the narrow xylem vessels, and this attraction helps counteract the downward pull of gravity on the water column and helps water climb the sides of the vessel, an effect closely related to capillary action, the tendency of water to rise on its own inside any sufficiently narrow tube.

Both properties trace back to the single fact introduced at the start of this chapter's chemistry sequence: carbon and its partners form bonds according to predictable rules of electron sharing and electronegativity, and when those rules are applied to a bent, polar molecule as small as water, the result is a hydrogen bonding network capable of moving water to the top of a tree, supporting the weight of an insect, and, as earlier sections of this course will go on to explore, dissolving and transporting the countless other molecules that make life possible.
